To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ROS, soot, PACs and allergenic proteins are hazardous components of atmospheric aerosols, and that their health effects are related to the generation of ROS in vivo.

(i) atmospheric ROS can trigger formation of oxidative DNA lesions in human bronchial epithelial cells; (ii) soot and PACs can induce ROS formation in vivo, leading in particular to oxidative DNA lesions; and (iii) allergenic proteins can be nitrated and nitrosated in the presence of ozone and nitrogen dioxide.

(1) ROS, soot, PACs and allergenic proteins are hazardous components of atmospheric aerosols, (2) ROS are key intermediates in the health effects of these components, (3) ROS are formed in vivo by the interaction of these components with physiological ROS sources such as ozone and NO2.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the elucidation of the chemical properties and molecular mechanisms of interaction of ROS, soot, PACs and allergenic proteins in order to understand the health effects of atmospheric particulate matter and to develop strategies to mitigate the adverse health effects of particulate pollution.
the chemical and biological properties of atmospheric aerosol components and their health effects.

the elucidation of the mechanisms and kinetics of multiphase reactions of ROS with organic and biological compounds in the gas, aqueous and solid phases, as well as the elucidation of mechanisms of oxidative stress in the lung and other organs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the health effects of atmospheric particles are not only determined by their mass, but also depend on their chemical composition and reactivity.
the oxidative stress induced by atmospheric aerosols is the key factor in aerosol health hazards.
the health effects of atmospheric particles are not due to a single compound, but are the result of a complex interaction of different compounds and reactive oxygen species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ROS and oxidatively modified proteins are important intermediates in the link between atmospheric multiphase chemistry and human health.

the health effects of atmospheric particles are mainly due to the oxidative stress caused by ROS, which are generated in a multiphase reaction chain initiated by photochemical and/or heterogeneous reactions in the troposphere.
the oxidative stress hypothesis for the adverse health effects of atmospheric particles is supported by recent research.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ROS are a central component of aerosol health effects.
ROS are key players in aerosol-induced adverse health effects and that the formation and reactivity of ROS in the atmosphere is closely linked with multiphase processes involving aerosol particles.
atmospheric aerosols contain a complex mixture of compounds with different physicochemical properties, which can interact with each other and with the human respiratory system.
